translation:
Among the five sense organs of the human body, only the ears and eyes are of the greatest importance, and apart from the function of hearing, nothing surpasses the function of seeing. Although the eye opens its orifice and belongs to the liver, the essence and fluids of the five viscera all ascend and pour into the eye, becoming its pupil. Hence the health-preservation masters have the doctrine of the quiet practice of inner vision, and the saying that the light of the eye shines like a candle at night. Only when inner nourishment is already full and external pathogens do not disturb it does the pupil remain clear and constantly bright. Yet in this world, who among men can avoid the toil of the mind and the labor of the body? If one is exposed to wind and frost, or invaded by summer heat, one is injured from without. If one harms the liver through pent-up anger, and the nutritive blood is exhausted, one is damaged from within. Thus if one wishes to treat the illness according to its cause, the lifelong matter of sight and blindness all issues from the hands of the physician—how can one fail to be cautious? Yet who in the world is he who can part the clouds and mist to behold the blue sky? If we set aside Master Deng of Qingjiang, with whom shall we return?

I once examined his Complete Book of Ophthalmology of the One-Grass Pavilion. In his own preface, the reason he took up medicine was based on the Song Confucian doctrine that a man who is a son must not be ignorant of medicine—thus he was a filial man. Moreover, he set his resolve and pledged himself to the aim of the Duke of Wenzheng, Fan Zhongyan, that if one cannot be a good minister, one should be a good physician—thus he was a benevolent man. When a benevolent and filial man devotes his full effort to medicine, how could he fail to reach the realm of the divine? Therefore, in establishing his theories and arranging his formulas, he distinguished internal depletion and external causes in full detail, and his prescriptions of odd and even numbers were precise, specialized, and complete. Moreover, what he transmitted far surpassed the ordinary by ten thousandfold. For this reason, whenever his formulas and medicines were used, they proved effective at every trial. It is a pity that the printing blocks were damaged and the book was not transmitted. I obtained this book and treasured it for a long time. Now I dare not keep it to myself, but entrust it again to the engraver and make it public to the world. This is not only to honor the painstaking effort of a benevolent and filial man in writing, but also so that all those in the world and in later ages who suffer from eye disease may select formulas, receive treatment, and regain their sight, without needing the practice of inner vision, and may of themselves preserve the most important of the five sense organs without fearing injury from wind, frost, or anger. Then how could the merit of Master Deng's One-Grass Pavilion be measured? This is my preface.

<ins>Written by Nian Xiyao of Guangning at the official residence in Jinling, in the ninth month of the dingyou year of the Kangxi reign</ins>
translator_notes: 司聰 (si cong) and 司明 (si ming) denote the functions of hearing and seeing respectively.
棗梨 (zaoli) refers to printing blocks; the phrase means the blocks were damaged.
剞劂 (jijue) means engraving, i.e., publication.
伊芳 is taken as a variant of 伊, meaning 'who'.
